lesson.title: Growth Genes with a Dark Side: Proto-Oncogenes
lesson.summary: Proto-oncogenes are normal genes that encode proteins promoting cell growth and division, and mutations that make them abnormally active turn them into oncogenes capable of driving cancer.
lesson.body:
Every gene that helps push a cell through the cycle, including the cyclins and CDKs described in the previous chapter, is a growth promoting gene. In its normal form, tightly regulated and turned on only when appropriate, a gene like this is called a proto-oncogene. The name reflects what happens when things go wrong: a proto-oncogene that becomes mutated or abnormally active is now called an oncogene, and an oncogene can drive a cell to divide even when it should not.

Proto-oncogenes encode a wide range of proteins involved in telling a cell to grow and divide: growth factors themselves, the receptors on the cell surface that detect growth factors, the signal transduction proteins that relay that detection into the cell, transcription factors that switch on division related genes, and, as covered in the previous chapter, cyclins and CDKs. A useful way to think about a proto-oncogene is as an accelerator pedal for the cell cycle. Pressed at the right time, in response to a real growth signal, it is exactly what a growing or repairing tissue needs.

The Ras protein is a well studied example. Ras is a signaling protein that normally cycles between an active, GTP bound state and an inactive, GDP bound state, relaying a growth factor signal from a cell surface receptor toward the nucleus only briefly before switching itself back off. A mutation in the ras gene can lock the Ras protein in its active state, so it keeps signaling for division continuously, with no growth factor required and no way to turn itself off. Mutated ras genes are found in a substantial fraction of human cancers, making Ras one of the most important oncogenes known.

Because an oncogene's protein is overactive on its own, a mutation in just one of a cell's two copies of the gene is often enough to cause a problem, since the abnormal, hyperactive protein produced from the mutant copy keeps driving the cell forward regardless of what the normal copy does. This is quite different from what happens with tumor suppressor genes, covered next, and the distinction between the two is one of the most important ideas in cancer biology. Oncogenic mutations can arise in several ways: a point mutation that changes a single amino acid, as with ras, amplification of the gene so that far more copies and far more protein are made than normal, or a chromosomal rearrangement that fuses part of one gene to another, as happens with the BCR-ABL fusion gene found in chronic myeloid leukemia, which creates a permanently active signaling enzyme out of two genes that are each normal on their own.
